data.title: Restriction of individual branched-chain amino acids has distinct effects on the development and progression of Alzheimer's disease in 3xTg mice
data.authors: Babygirija R; Lamming DW et al.

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: UPDATE (was bioRxiv preprint at seed time, peer-reviewed and published in Advanced Science March 2026). Restricting individual branched-chain amino acids has distinct, sex-specific effects on cognition and AD pathology in 3xTg mice; restriction of isoleucine and valine (but not leucine) promotes metabolic health. Note: the different BCAAs act differentially on mTORC1, which is why single-amino-acid restriction matters.
data.abstract_excerpt: Dietary protein regulates metabolic health and aging, with many benefits of a low protein diet resulting from reduced consumption of the three branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), leucine, isoleucine, and valine. Each BCAA has distinct physiological and molecular effects, and while restriction of protein or all three BCAAs improves cognition in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease (AD), the role of each individual BCAA on AD is unknown.

extracted_findings.effect: Individual BCAAs have distinct, sex-specific effects on Alzheimer's progression; restricting any BCAA improved short-term memory in males (isoleucine strongest), while valine restriction gave the largest cognitive benefit in females
extracted_findings.dose: Diets with 67% reduction of isoleucine, leucine, or valine, started at 6 months of age; duration was 9 months for body composition, 3 months for metabolic tests.
extracted_findings.sample_size: 3xTg and NTg mice of both sexes; n=5-14 per diet group per sex, varying by experiment.
extracted_findings.effect_size: ValR diet significantly increased energy expenditure in 3xTg females (p<0.05); IleR increased energy expenditure in 3xTg males (p<0.05) and improved glucose tolerance in both sexes (p<0.05).
